name: AI trade jitters
backstory: Markets have leaned on the biggest AI-linked tech firms, so doubts about AI hit the whole [[S&P 500]]. Nvidia's CEO left on Nov 12, a selloff followed, official papers warned that AI [[valuation]]s look stretched, and the index fell four straight weeks.
today: Nvidia's board approved Huang's return, and Reuters reports that Trump pressured the company to do it. The Nasdaq rose 6.51% and the S&P 500 had its best day in more than a year, while Oracle and CoreWeave also jumped because cloud companies like them, along with Nebius and Iren, depend on Nvidia's financing of the AI ecosystem. The cheering came with pushback, because lawmakers of both parties questioned Trump's conclusion that Huang is not a national security risk, Treasury Secretary Bessent reversed his harder line on Nvidia, staff abuse allegations surfaced and a reported SEC probe is in the news. A strategist also warned that Wall Street is not pricing in a [[data center]] slowdown, and HPE posted its strongest growth ever and raised its forecast, yet its stock wavered, which hints that good news is already expected.

name: Central banks vs energy inflation
backstory: The Iran war cut oil supply and pushed up [[headline inflation]], so central banks must decide whether the price jump fades or leaks into wages and services. Euro area inflation hit 4%, the Bank of England hiked to 4% and the Fed sits at 3.875%.
today: Fed's John Williams said higher interest rates are likely 'over time' to address inflation, but he is confident inflation gets closer to 2% in 2027. Waller said the Fed meets Dec 8 and 9, with the economic outlook discussed on the first day and the policy decision on the second. Cook said damaged infrastructure and low inventories could keep oil prices high for a long time, and Japan's core inflation hit its highest this year as an energy subsidy ended. Meanwhile Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh is described as seeing an AI revolution coming that raises hard questions on jobs and interest rates.

name: Iran war and oil
backstory: The conflict began in early 2026 and cut global oil output by 12 mb/d in March, but prices stayed below records because stored oil filled the gap. The IEA says the Hormuz shock lifted the world's oil and gas import bill 25% to $1.6 trillion.
today: [[WTI crude]] fell 4.23% to 80.43, its lowest close since August, because oil kept flowing out of the Persian Gulf even though tanker attacks continue. A headline says China has become the top oil buyer. Trump suggested the recent drop in gas prices is driven by political forces now that the midterms are over, and a headline puts the phrase 'a giant hoax' on it.

name: US midterms and the dollar
backstory: The midterms produced what headlines call a Democratic rout, and markets asked how divided government might change tariffs, spending and the [[dollar index]]. The dollar then had its biggest rally since 2024.
today: The dollar index rose 0.49% to 104.32, and headlines credit hawkish Fed bets, not the election. Goldman Sachs expects the rally to continue in the coming months and fade in 2027, though its technical read says the dollar is [[overbought]] and could slow. Sterling and the euro edged up in the morning as the stock rebound took some of the shine off the dollar, but the dollar was higher again by the close.

name: Yen defense
backstory: A weak yen pushed Japan to intervene [sell dollars to buy yen] in the currency market, including a record $50 billion in one day. The BOJ's 1.25% rate is 2.625 percentage points below the Fed's 3.875%, which encourages selling yen to hold dollars. Japan's economy unexpectedly shrank in Q3 as energy costs bit.
today: USD/JPY was 159.32, down 0.04%, so the yen was little changed. The BOJ chief played down soft consumption data and signaled a near-term rate hike. Japan's inflation accelerated, and the country posted a sixth straight monthly trade deficit. A Reuters-style analysis says BOJ ambiguity on the path of hikes could tempt yen bears. In Friday's Asian session, the Nikkei fell 2.9% on chip and metals stocks.
